text.text: If confirmed, this asymmetry would be a substantive contribution of the person-centered longitudinal design adopted here: a single-wave, person-centered analysis can show that qualitatively distinct configurations of practice exist, and variable-centered longitudinal models can separate predictors of initial levels from predictors of change in single dimensions of technology use; the person-centered longitudinal design adds the possibility of relating predictors to membership in, and movement between, qualitatively distinct configurations of practice.

The present study has several limitations: First, the small number of countries that participated in the ICILS 2018-2020 teacher panel study limits, on the one hand, the degree of generalizability of the technology utilization profiles.
Whether these profiles replicate in other systems, and whether additional profile types exist that the three-country sample does not reveal, remain open questions.

An extended multi-country panel study could address both replicability and heterogeneity while also linking profile structures to system-level characteristics such as national digitalization policies or teacher education programs.
Second, the measures in ICILS 2018 and 2020 focused on technology in general, despite some specification of broad categories.
Specific technologies, such as artificial intelligence or virtual environments, had not been considered.
Follow-up ICILS cycles, however, have included or will be including some of them, yet with cross-sectional designs (Fraillon & Rožman, 2025; IEA, 2026).
text.formatted: Follow-up ICILS cycles, however, have included or will be including some of them, yet with cross-sectional designs <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Fraillon & Rožman, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">IEA, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These datasets will provide opportunities to examine more specific technology utilization profiles and their possible impacts in education.
Third, using alignment-based factor scores as observed profile indicators does not propagate their measurement error into the LPA and LTA steps.

This limitation is particularly relevant for CODEMP and UTOOLC, where fit and invariance were weakest (see Table 2), and may affect the precision of profile solutions in which these indicators are primary discriminators.

text.text: Fourth, restricting the sample to panel completers could introduce attrition bias.

Comparisons with eligible baseline-only teachers showed no significant differences in Denmark, while completers were older, more experienced, and somewhat lower in ICT self-efficacy in Finland, and scored higher on self-efficacy, collaboration, and professional development in Uruguay.

Tracking-status information needed to identify ineligible teachers was complete for Finland but substantially incomplete for Denmark and Uruguay, so some residual, unidentifiable ineligibility may remain in those two countries' comparison groups.

Attrition therefore was not entirely random: the analytic sample may over-represent older and more experienced teachers in Finland and teachers with higher ICT self-efficacy, collaboration, and professional development participation in Uruguay, which may modestly limit generalizability.
Fifth, our profile indicators relied on teacher self-reports of ICT use, which may be subject to social desirability or recall bias and may not fully correspond to observed classroom practice.
Future work could benefit from complementing self-report with classroom observation or log-file data.
Sixth, our analyses were based on only two measurement occasions (2018 and 2020).

While this design allows us to model transitions in teachers' technology utilization profiles, it does not permit examination of longer-term trajectories, non-linear patterns of change, or the stability of profiles beyond this two-year window.

Seventh, the "emphasis-practice gap" profiles (the Finnish "constrained integrators" and the Uruguayan "aspirational non-users") were identified using ICTEMP and CODEMP, which capture teachers' pedagogical emphasis on ICT and coding capabilities rather than direct psychological measures of attitudes (e.g., perceived usefulness, enjoyment).

ICILS did not include such direct attitudinal measures, so this interpretation could not be validated post-hoc; this distinction should be kept in mind when relating our findings to attitude-based frameworks, such as the TAM.
Eighth, the eight profile indicators did not contribute equally to profile identification.
In Finland, the profile structure could not be estimated due to non-convergence when CODEMP and UTOOLC were excluded jointly.
For the 2020 assessment, the exclusion of UTOOLC alone was sufficient to reproduce this non-convergence (see Section 4.2.6).
The Finnish typology therefore relied heavily on the joint presence of these specific indicators.
This may limit the application of the profile typology in future studies that use a reduced or different set of indicators of teachers' technology utilization.
It also underlines the value of retaining coding emphasis and content-creation tool use when profiling teachers' technology utilization.

Similarly, excluding UTOOLL changed individual transition probabilities in Denmark and Uruguay appreciably (maximum cell shifts of .187 and .328), so that estimates of mobility between specific profiles in these countries depend on the indicator set and should be interpreted with caution.
Ninth, profile enumeration required judgment where the information criteria and the other selection criteria disagreed.
Most notably, the BIC favored four profiles in Finland at T1 under both specifications (ΔBIC = 154 and 168).

We retained three profiles because the four-profile solutions were not reproducible across specifications (see Section 4.2.1), but a finer differentiation of the Finnish profiles at T1 cannot be ruled out.
Similar discrepancies between the BIC and the other criteria occurred for Denmark at T1 and Uruguay at T2.
Replications with larger or independent samples could clarify whether additional profiles exist.

This study provides large-scale and longitudinal evidence on the typological structure and temporal dynamics of teachers' ICT utilization using data from three countries across two measurement occasions.

By taking a person-centered longitudinal approach, the study extends existing research on teachers' ICT utilization by demonstrating that teachers' technology-related practices differ qualitatively in how digital technologies are used in classroom practice.

Taken together, the study demonstrates the value of person-centered longitudinal approaches for understanding the complexity and developmental dynamics of digital teaching practices across educational systems.
The findings of the present study suggest that professional development initiatives should move beyond generic, one-size-fits-all models of ICT training.

Because teachers' ICT utilization differs qualitatively, professional support may need to be differentiated to match teachers' specific profiles and practices-with foundational access support for minimally engaged teachers, support in translating pedagogical emphasis into classroom practice for teachers who combine a high pedagogical emphasis on ICT with comparatively limited classroom implementation, and pedagogical deepening for functional integrators.
Whether such profilespecific support is more effective than generic training remains to be tested.

Separately from these profile-specific needs, the association between collaborative ICT use and profile membership in all three countries suggests that fostering collaboration around ICT may support teachers' technology utilization more broadly, although our design cannot establish such an effect.

The results also suggest that professional development related to advanced digital competencies, including coding and content creation, should be designed with greater attention to potential gender disparities in teachers' engagement and confidence.
Schools and policymakers should therefore ensure that opportunities to develop advanced ICT-related pedagogical skills are equally accessible and supportive across teacher groups.

Finally, the findings indicate that digital education policies should recognize that technology integration is shaped by local curricular priorities, institutional conditions, professional cultures, and broader national approaches to digitalization.
Policies and implementation strategies may therefore be more effective when adapted to the specific contextual realities of individual educational systems and schools.

text.text: This person-centered panel design offers three analytical advantages: it captures multidimensional ICT utilization profiles rather than single composite scores; it tracks whether profiles are stable or changing across occasions; and it links individual and contextual characteristics to both profile membership and transitions.
Specifically, we address the following research questions (RQs): RQ1.
Which latent profiles of teachers' technology utilization exist and what characterizes them?
(Unobserved teacher profiles) RQ2.
To what extent do teachers transition between these profiles over time?
(Transitions between profiles) RQ3.

To what extent are teacher characteristics (i.e., age, gender, experience, selfefficacy, perceived resources and collaboration, engagement in professional development, and view on technology) related to latent profile membership and the transitions over time?
(Covariates of profile membership and transitions)
